clue.text: Swear Sheeran's back with model

indicators.note: the singer's name read from the back means its letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: Ed Sheeran, the singer, gives his first name
to model is to pose for an artist

explanation.surface: Someone cursing that the pop star Ed Sheeran has returned to his model girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear' looks like cursing, but here it means to testify on oath.
explanation.definitionFit: To depose is to give sworn testimony, a legal synonym for swearing under oath.

clue.text: Labour supporter

parts.note: surface reading: someone who backs the British Labour Party
setter's reading: a person who supports a woman giving birth

explanation.walkthrough: Labour is the UK's main left-wing party, so the clue reads as a political voter; the capital L hides childbirth.
explanation.definitionFit: A doula is a trained companion who gives non-medical support to a mother during childbirth.

clue.text: Duck eaten by dramatist's dog

indicators.note: something eaten ends up inside whatever eats it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Harold Pinter, the English playwright
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A playwright's dog has eaten a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointer is a breed of gun dog that stands still and points towards game.

clue.text: Tears prey apart for fat

indicators.note: torn apart means pulled to pieces, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A predator rips its victim to pieces to get at the fat.
explanation.walkthrough: A spare tyre is British slang for a roll of fat round the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare tyre is an informal name for a bulge of body fat around the midriff.

clue.text: Taxi driver might not keep quiet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fasten a seatbelt, which UK taxi drivers are exempt from doing when carrying passengers
second meaning: a rude British instruction to shut up

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a chatty cabbie; in Britain taxi drivers need not wear seatbelts, and the same phrase is slang for shut up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both fastening a seatbelt and, colloquially, falling silent.

clue.text: Raise editor's case with English court

indicators.note: a case is the outside shell of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of editor
standard abbreviation for English
standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: An editor's legal case is raised in an English court.
explanation.definitionFit: To erect a building or a mast is to raise it up; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Sailors with second bit of meat served raw

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, so two sailors make a pair of tars

indicators.note: the second bit of a word is its second letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the second letter of meat

explanation.surface: Sailors are given a second helping of meat that is served uncooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Tar is old slang for a sailor; the plural is supplied by two of them side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartare describes a dish, such as steak tartare, of finely chopped meat or fish eaten uncooked.

clue.text: I prefer to badly overcharge

indicators.note: something done badly is botched and disordered, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper admits he likes to rip customers off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I prefer' reads as a personal admission, but every letter of 'I prefer to' is reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: To profiteer is to make excessive profits, typically by charging inflated prices in a shortage.

clue.text: Joke about educated woman, a prude

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a pun is a joke on words
Rita is the heroine of Willy Russell's play Educating Rita

explanation.surface: A prudish person makes a joke at the expense of a learned woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita is a well-known British play and film about a hairdresser going to university.
explanation.definitionFit: A puritan is someone with strict moral views who disapproves of pleasure, much like a prude.

clue.text: Teacher fell over in sleeping quarters

parts.note: a BEd, Bachelor of Education, is a teaching degree

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a fell is a stretch of upland moor in northern England

explanation.surface: A teacher tripped and fell over in the dormitory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' looks like the past tense of fall; it is the noun for a hill or moor.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedroom is the room where one sleeps, so it is literally a person's sleeping quarters.

clue.text: Foreign force tired out but showing courage

parts.note: F is the symbol for force in physics

indicators.note: foreign means strange and unfamiliar, so the following letters appear in an altered order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An overseas army is exhausted yet still brave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign force' reads as an army, but the first word is the signal to rearrange 'tired out', and force alone is F.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortitude is strength of mind that lets someone endure hardship, essentially courage.

clue.text: Sad old starlets drinking last of liquor — no other option

indicators.note: whatever is drunk goes inside the drinker, so one piece sits within the other
sad here means sorry or in a sorry state, so the letters are in disarray

parts.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
taken as written

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of liquor

explanation.surface: Washed-up actresses turning to drink because they have nothing else left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sad old' reads as a description of the starlets, but old only supplies O, which joins the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A last resort is the final course of action open when everything else has failed.

clue.text: Aussie occasionally beginning to flip? I don't believe you

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of Aussie

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of flip

explanation.surface: An Australian now and then starts to lose their temper, scoffing at what they hear.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a scornful retort expressing disbelief, the same idiom as saying you don't believe it.

clue.text: Tory perhaps not completely left out

indicators.note: out means removed or excluded, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: partly means to some extent but not completely
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician who is not entirely left out of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tory, or Conservative, Party is one of Britain's two main political parties.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tories form a political party, so Tory serves as an example of the category, signalled by perhaps.

clue.text: Drunk did some decorating

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for very intoxicated
second meaning: covered a wall with smooth lime or gypsum coating

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a tipsy decorator; the two halves are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for very intoxicated and also the past tense of applying a wall coating.

clue.text: Restrained delinquent youth inhaling solvent

indicators.note: what is inhaled is taken inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth known for rowdiness
ether is a volatile solvent

explanation.surface: A young offender caught sniffing solvents was held back.
explanation.definitionFit: Tethered means tied by a rope or chain, physically restrained from moving freely.

clue.text: Woman berating dreadful German tat

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a terrible state, so these letters are messed up and reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman complains loudly about some awful German junk; tat is British slang for cheap tasteless goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is an old word for a harsh, overbearing, scolding woman.

clue.text: Money for campaign backing Green case

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: green and raw both mean inexperienced
a chest is a large case or box

explanation.surface: Funding for a political campaign that supports the Green Party's case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like the environmentalist party; it means inexperienced.
explanation.definitionFit: A war chest is a fund of money built up to fight a campaign, originally a military one.

clue.text: Liberal ignoring entire contest

indicators.note: to ignore is to leave out of account, so a letter is removed

parts.note: entire and complete are synonyms
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A Liberal candidate snubs the whole election contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To compete is to take part in a contest, to vie with rivals for a prize.

clue.text: Bishop embracing great competitor on track

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: RR stands for Right Reverend, a bishop's title
ace means excellent or great

explanation.surface: A bishop hugs a great athlete at the racetrack.
explanation.definitionFit: A racer is someone or something that takes part in races, a competitor on a running or motor track.

clue.text: Friendly drink

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a sweet fruit-flavoured beverage, often diluted

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a sociable drink; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for warm courteous manner and a noun for a sweetened fruit syrup beverage.

clue.text: Couple I ran into travelling west

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means moving right to left, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: to run into someone is to meet them

explanation.surface: Someone bumped into a pair of people while journeying west.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is informal for a couple in a romantic relationship, as in 'they are an item'.

clue.text: Finding Bob intractable on this occasion?

definitions.text: Finding Bob intractable on this occasion?

parts.words: Finding Bob intractable on this occasion?
parts.note: surface reading: a time when a man called Bob is being stubborn
setter's reading: a bob is a short haircut, so one's hairstyle refuses to behave

explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a man's name, but it is a haircut; the answer is the idiom for a day when your hair won't do as it is told.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a day when one's hair looks unmanageable, and by extension a day when everything goes wrong.

clue.text: Bank of Scotland welcoming Conservative's support

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: brae is the Scots word for a hillside or bank
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: The Bank of Scotland is welcoming backing from the Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank of Scotland' reads as the financial institution, but it means a Scottish word for a bank, as in a hillside.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a strut or prop that holds something steady, so it is a structural support.

clue.text: A sub reportedly abandoned

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: a sub is a small advance of money, that is, a loan

explanation.surface: A submarine is said to have been deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sub' suggests a submarine or substitute; it is an advance on wages.
explanation.definitionFit: To be left alone is to be on one's own, deserted by others, matching abandoned.

clue.text: Squad with no shortage of firepower?

definitions.text: Squad with no shortage of firepower?

parts.words: Squad with no shortage of firepower?
parts.note: surface reading: a military unit well stocked with guns
setter's reading: a London football team nicknamed the Gunners, whose name also means a weapons store

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an army unit; it is the London football club whose name is also a stockpile of weapons, and whose nickname is the Gunners.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a store of weapons and the name of a famous North London football club.

clue.text: Doorman Victor half-cut on New Year's day

parts.note: the first of January, written as JAN I

indicators.note: cut by half means half of the word is chopped away

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A doorman called Victor was drunk on New Year's Day; half-cut is British slang for tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut' reads as drunk, which fits New Year, but it says to lose half of Victor.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor is a caretaker of a building, originally a doorkeeper, from Latin janua, door.

clue.text: One watching weight put off hosting Moo

indicators.note: a host has guests within, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to put off is to discourage, or deter
Moo is the setter, who refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: Someone on a diet is put off by having to entertain a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: Moo is this puzzle's setter, so the name stands for I, the setter speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A dieter restricts food intake to lose pounds, so they are someone keeping an eye on their weight.

clue.text: British losing fight with European PM

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter is removed

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a battle is a fight
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A British prime minister loses a political fight with Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was the Labour Prime Minister of Britain from 1945 to 1951.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee led the post-war Labour government, so he is an example of a Prime Minister.
